doc: On-device search: route classification for the filter chips, the smart keypad's valid-next-key lookup, and the two search functions (ADR-037). All pure and platform-free, which is what makes the index queryable offline. **Nothing in this file may use a locale collator** — that is ADR-063's whole point: `localeCompare(numeric:true)` has no faithful Swift/Kotlin equivalent, so ordering is a byte comparison of a zero-padded `routeSortKey` and the keypad is a range scan over a byte-sorted array. A port that reaches for ICU here has reintroduced the defect even if every row below still passes. Conventions for this file: (1) `routeKeys`, `nextValidChars` and `isCompleteRoute` cases give `routeNos`; the latter two build the key array from them first. (2) `nextValidChars` returns a SET; cases express it as a SORTED array, so a port must sort before comparing rather than assume iteration order. (3) The two search functions take whole records but `expect` only the resulting ids, in result order. (4) `compareRouteNo` cases expect the SIGN of the comparison (-1, 0, 1). The implementation now returns exactly those three values, but a port may return any signed integer, so compare signs.

routeCategories.doc: Which filter categories a route number belongs to, derived from the number alone — no lookup, no dataset. A route can belong to several. The returned order is fixed: night, then airport, then express. Matching is case-insensitive. Night = leading N. Airport/Lantau = the A/NA/E/S families, which require a DIGIT after the letters. Express = an X anywhere in the number.

cases.name: night-airport-service
cases.why: NA10 is both: it leads with N and matches the NA family with a digit. Proves the categories are additive, and pins the array ORDER as night-before-airport.

cases.name: bare-na-is-night-only
cases.why: The family patterns require a digit, so a bare 'NA' is night only — even though src/search.ts's own comment offers 'NA' as the night+airport example. No such route number exists (the real ones are NA10, NA11, NA20), so this is a doc inaccuracy rather than a behavioural bug. Recorded so a port reading that comment does not 'correct' the regex and quietly reclassify things.

cases.name: a-single-letter-matches-no-family
cases.why: 'A' alone has no digit, so it is uncategorized. Same rule as the bare-NA row.

cases.name: express-suffix
cases.why: The X test is `includes`, not a suffix test — 269X and X1 both qualify.

cases.name: night-and-express
cases.why: NX would be both. Pins the order as night-before-express.

cases.name: lower-case-input-is-upper-cased-first
cases.why: Reachable: the text search path passes whatever the rider typed.

routeMatchesFilter.doc: Whether a route passes the active filter. The two axes AND together; selections WITHIN an axis OR together. An empty array on an axis means no restriction on that axis — NOT 'match nothing', which is the mistake worth guarding.

cases.name: axes-and-together-so-one-failure-rejects
cases.why: A night route, but the wrong operator. Passing one axis is not enough.

stopMatchesOperators.doc: Whether a stop or place id involves any of the given operators. Places are pre-merged on the edge into a self-describing id — `P:` followed by member canonical ids joined by `+` — so the operators of a place are read straight out of its id with no lookup. An empty operator list means no restriction.

cases.name: four-member-place-any-member-operator
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW (a 4-member place). Clustering has been N-member since ADR-042, so a two-member fixture proves nothing about the general case. This id has FOUR members across THREE operators, including two poles of the same operator: `P:CTB:002451+GMB:HK1234+KMB:ST141+KMB:ST142`. Filtering by GMB must match on the THIRD member, so a port that only inspects the id's prefix, or only the first member, passes a two-member fixture and fails here.

cases.name: four-member-place-repeated-member-operator
cases.why: Two of the four poles are KMB. One match is enough; nothing counts occurrences.

cases.name: four-member-place-absent-operator
cases.why: LWB serves no pole of this place. Note LWB is a distinct operator from KMB in the canonical model even though they share a feed.

cases.name: the-operator-code-must-be-followed-by-a-colon
cases.why: A raw stop code that merely contains an operator's letters must not match: 'KMB:CTB999' is a KMB pole whose upstream code happens to read CTB. The colon is what makes the test a code test rather than a substring test.

routeKeys.doc: Every route number the keypad can reach, upper-cased, de-duplicated and BYTE-sorted — the array that replaced the prefix trie in ADR-063. Byte order, not rider order: contiguity of a prefix is what makes the range scans below work, and only a plain code-unit sort gives it. Blank numbers are dropped. Route numbers are `[0-9A-Z]`, where a UTF-16 code-unit sort, Swift's `<` and Kotlin's `compareTo` all agree; a port must NOT substitute a locale-aware sort.

cases.name: a-route-and-its-own-prefix
cases.why: '1' is both a real route and a prefix of '1A'. Both survive as separate entries, and the shorter sorts first — which is what lets `isCompleteRoute` say 'submit is meaningful' for '1' while `nextValidChars` still offers 'A'. The trie expressed this as a node that was terminal AND had children; a port modelling terminality as 'a leaf' got it wrong, and the array form cannot make that mistake.

cases.name: duplicates-collapse
cases.why: Case-folding happens before de-duplication, so '1A' and '1a' are one key, not two. The edge collapses service-type variants but the same number can still arrive twice across operators.

cases.name: branching-numbers-share-a-prefix
cases.why: '10' before '1A' because '0' (U+0030) precedes 'A' (U+0041). Digits sorting ahead of letters is not a convention this code chose — it is ASCII, and it is why the same array works in three languages.

cases.name: the-array-is-in-byte-order-not-rider-order
cases.why: '10' before '2', which is the OPPOSITE of what a rider should see in a results list. Deliberate, and the one row most likely to be 'fixed' by mistake: sorting this array by `routeSortKey` would put '0002' between '0001' and '0010' and break the contiguity every range scan depends on. Display order is `searchRoutes`'s job, and it is a different order.

cases.name: a-blank-route-number-is-dropped
cases.why: FIXED 2026-07-28 under the trie, preserved here. An empty string used to mark the trie's ROOT terminal, making `isCompleteRoute(root, '')` true and telling the keypad that submitting an empty query was meaningful. A blank is also a prefix of everything, so keeping it would make the whole index the answer to a query nobody typed. Unreachable today — the edge index emits none — but nothing rejects one, so a bad dataset build would arm it.

nextValidChars.doc: The characters that, appended to `prefix`, still lead to a real route — the smart keypad's live key-enabling. Cases give `routeNos` (build the key array with `routeKeys` first) and `prefix`; `expect` is the sorted set. A range scan, not a trie walk (ADR-063): binary-search the first key ≥ prefix, then take the next character of each key until one no longer carries the prefix. The prefix is upper-cased. A prefix that leads nowhere yields the empty set, never an error.

cases.name: a-complete-route-with-no-continuation-offers-nothing
cases.why: '1A' is a real route and nothing extends it, so every key goes dead. Distinct from a dead prefix — the keypad must enable submit here but no keys.

cases.name: a-dead-prefix-offers-nothing
cases.why: 'Z' matches no route at all. Empty, not an error — the keypad never lets a rider reach this, but the text field can.

isCompleteRoute.doc: Whether the prefix is itself a complete route number, so submitting it is meaningful. A prefix of a real route is NOT complete. One binary search for exact membership in the `routeKeys` array; the empty prefix answers false with no special case, because blanks never enter the array.

cases.name: the-empty-prefix-is-not-a-route
cases.why: Submitting nothing must never be meaningful. Contrast the blank-route-number defect recorded under buildRouteTrie, which is exactly what would break this.

indexAlphabet.doc: The digits and letters appearing anywhere in the dataset's route numbers, each sorted ascending, so the keypad renders a stable layout of only the keys this dataset can ever use. Anything that is neither an ASCII digit nor an A-Z letter is dropped.

cases.name: punctuation-is-dropped
cases.why: A hyphen is neither a digit nor a letter, so no key is offered for it.

routeSortKey.doc: A byte-comparable ordering key for a route number: every run of digits is zero-padded to FOUR, so `10A` → `0010A` and `9` < `10A` < `11` under plain byte comparison. This is ADR-063's core move — the order stops being a computation (`localeCompare(numeric:true)`, which Swift and Kotlin cannot reproduce faithfully) and becomes a property of the string, which every language compares identically. The edge precomputes it into `RouteLite.sortKey`; this function is both the definition and the client's fallback, so the two can never disagree. Input is upper-cased (replacing the old collator's `sensitivity: 'base'`), and leading zeros disappear into the padding. A digit run LONGER than four is prefixed with one `~` per extra digit rather than padded: `~` (U+007E) sorts after every digit and every upper-case letter, so a longer run always sorts after a shorter one and equal lengths compare lexically — which for equal lengths is numeric order. Hong Kong has no such route number today; the rule exists because the input is upstream data we do not control.

cases.name: the-canonical-example
cases.why: `10A` → `0010A` is the transformation docs/proposals/03 names for this work package. Everything else follows from it.

cases.name: night-prefix-keeps-its-letter-in-front
cases.why: The letter is not part of the numeric run, so `N260` keys as `N0260` and lands after every bare number — which is where riders expect night services.

cases.name: letters-on-both-sides-of-the-digits
cases.why: `E22A` has a leading letter, a numeric run and a trailing letter. A port that only pads a LEADING run of digits produces `E22A` unchanged and silently orders the whole E family wrong.

cases.name: lower-case-folds-up
cases.why: So `10a` and `10A` key identically and compare equal, which is what the old collator's `sensitivity: 'base'` bought and what `searchRoutes` relies on for its operator tiebreak to decide.

cases.name: leading-zeros-vanish-into-the-padding
cases.why: An upstream `007` must not become a second identity alongside `7`. Padding makes them the same key rather than requiring a separate normalization step nobody would port.

cases.name: a-five-digit-run-overflows-the-width
cases.why: The width is four; a longer run gets one `~` per extra digit instead. `9999` < `~10000` because `9` (U+0039) precedes `~` (U+007E) — which is numerically right, where leaving the run unpadded would have put 12345 before 9999.

cases.name: a-six-digit-run-overflows-further
cases.why: The marker repeats, so `~99999` (five digits) still sorts before `~~100000` (six). One `~` per extra digit is what keeps overflow CORRECT rather than merely deterministic.

cases.name: punctuation-passes-through
cases.why: A hyphen is neither a digit nor a letter and is simply copied, so a malformed number still yields a usable key rather than throwing. It sorts before every digit, which is as good a place as any for something that should not exist.

compareRouteNo.doc: Natural comparison of route numbers, so a rider sees 2 before 10 rather than 10 before 2. Since ADR-063 this is a BYTE comparison of two `routeSortKey` values, not a collator call — do not port it as `compare(options: .numeric)` or a hand-rolled natural comparator, because the point of the change is that those three implementations disagreed. Case-insensitive by way of the key's upper-casing. `expect` is the SIGN: the implementation returns exactly -1/0/1, but a port may return any signed integer.

cases.name: numeric-not-lexical
cases.why: The whole reason this function exists. Comparing the raw strings puts '10' before '2'; comparing their keys ('0010' and '0002') does not.

cases.name: a-lettered-variant-sorts-after-a-smaller-bare-number
cases.why: The ordering docs/proposals/03 states for this work package, half one: 9 < 10A. Keys '0009' and '0010A'.

cases.name: a-lettered-variant-sorts-before-the-next-bare-number
cases.why: Half two: 10A < 11. Keys '0010A' and '0011'. Together with the row above this pins 9 < 10A < 11, which is the whole claim the sort key exists to make true on three platforms at once.

cases.name: a-letter-prefix-sorts-after-a-bare-number
cases.why: Night routes land at the end of the list, which is what riders expect.

cases.name: case-is-not-significant
cases.why: Equal, not merely close. searchRoutes relies on this returning 0 so its secondary operator comparison decides the order.

normalizeRouteQuery.doc: Normalize a typed route query from the keypad or the text field: trim, then upper-case. Nothing else — no stripping of punctuation, no collapsing of internal spaces.

cases.name: whitespace-only-normalizes-to-empty
cases.why: Which searchRoutes then treats as 'no query', returning nothing rather than everything.

searchRoutes.doc: Routes whose number begins with the normalized query and pass the filter, sorted by number then operator. An EMPTY query returns NOTHING — deliberately, so an empty search box shows an empty state instead of the entire network. `expect` is the resulting ids in order. Both sort axes are byte comparisons (ADR-063): the number by `sortKey` — the edge's precomputed value where there is one, else `routeSortKey` of the number — and the operator code directly. Ties must keep index order, so a port needs a STABLE sort (Swift's `sorted(by:)` is not stable — use an index tiebreak).

cases.name: prefix-match-sorted-by-number-then-operator
cases.why: Three routes start with '1'. 10 sorts before 10A; the two 10s tie on number, so the operator breaks it and CTB comes before KMB.

cases.name: empty-query-returns-nothing
cases.why: Not 'everything'. A port that treats an empty prefix as matching all would dump the network into the results list.

cases.name: both-filter-axes-apply-together
cases.why: Query '2' matches both a plain KMB route and an express one; the category axis keeps only the express.

cases.name: limit-truncates-after-sorting
cases.why: The limit is applied to the SORTED list, so it keeps the routes a rider most expects, not the first two the index happened to hold.

cases.name: circular-route-blank-en-found-by-number
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW (empty `en` on a circular route). Upstream really ships GMB circular services with a blank English origin/destination while the Chinese reads '大角咀(循環線)' — the '(CIRCULAR)' marker that ADR-046 detects to suppress the direction toggle. Route search must be unaffected, because it matches on the NUMBER and never reads the name: a rider on an English UI can still find route 2 even though the app has no English words to show for either end of it. The row exists so nobody 'improves' route search into a name search and thereby makes blank-`en` routes unfindable in English — a regression no schema could catch, since a blank string is a perfectly valid string.

cases.name: the-edge-sort-key-decides-the-order
cases.why: The two `sortKey`s are deliberately the reverse of what the numbers imply, so this row can only pass if the client sorts by the field the edge sent rather than re-deriving one from `routeNo`. That is the property that makes the displayed order a dataset publish instead of three client releases (WP3-4), and it is invisible in any row where the two agree.

cases.name: a-route-with-no-sort-key-derives-one
cases.why: `sortKey` is optional on the wire (ADR-052 §5), so an index cached before the field existed, or served by an older edge, must still sort. Route 10 carries an edge key of '0099'; route 12 carries none and derives '0012', which sorts first. Mixing the two sources in one comparison is the case a port is most likely to get wrong by deriving everything or trusting everything.

cases.name: same-number-same-operator-keeps-index-order
cases.why: GMB public numbers repeat across regions, so route 1 genuinely exists in both Hong Kong Island and the New Territories as two separate services (ADR-047). They tie on BOTH sort axes — same key, same operator code — so the only thing deciding their order is the sort's stability. Swift's is not stable, and an unstable port reshuffles these two between keystrokes for no visible reason.

searchStops.doc: Stops and places whose name contains the query in ANY locale, so a Chinese rider and an English rider both find a stop regardless of the UI language. A prefix match ranks above a mid-string match; ties keep index order, which means a port needs a STABLE sort (Swift's `sorted(by:)` is not stable — use an index tiebreak). The query is trimmed and lower-cased on both sides. An empty query returns nothing. The operator filter, if any, is applied through the id. `expect` is the resulting ids in order.

cases.name: prefix-ranks-above-mid-string
cases.why: Both names contain 'city'; the one that STARTS with it comes first, even though it is second in the index.

cases.name: equal-rank-keeps-index-order
cases.why: Two prefix matches must come back in index order, which requires a STABLE sort. Swift's sort is not stable, so a naive port can flip these two and the results list reshuffles between keystrokes for no visible reason.

cases.name: circular-route-blank-en-found-by-chinese-name
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW (empty `en` on a circular route). The GMB circular terminus whose English name upstream is an empty string. Two things must hold at once: the Chinese query finds it, AND the active locale is `en` — so the candidate list must fall through the two blank English entries to the Chinese ones. A port that reads only the active locale's name, or that treats a blank name as a reason to skip the stop entirely, makes this stop unsearchable for the majority of HK riders, who type Chinese. That is why the row is not decorative: the blank is in the field the code looks at FIRST.

cases.name: a-blank-en-cannot-be-matched-by-an-english-query
cases.why: The honest converse of the row above: there is no English name, so an English query finds nothing. A port must NOT make a blank name match everything, which is what an unguarded `indexOf` on an empty candidate would do.

cases.name: four-member-place-appears-once
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW (a 4-member place). The edge pre-merges a same-kerb group into ONE index row carrying a 4-member `P:` id, so a query returns one result for the place, not one per pole — and the id the rider navigates to is the whole place. A port that re-derived rows per member would show the same kerb four times.

cases.name: four-member-place-passes-a-third-member-operator-filter
cases.why: The GMB filter must reach the place through its THIRD member id. Pairs the stopMatchesOperators row with the search path that actually calls it.

cases.name: a-simplified-query-matches-the-simplified-name
cases.why: The candidate list covers all three locales, so a Simplified reader finds a stop whose Traditional and Simplified names differ.
